# How to Build a Clean Invoice and Payment Tracker in Excel with Copilot

> **In short:** You can use Copilot in Excel to build an invoice tracker by asking it to create columns, write formulas, and highlight overdue rows in plain English — but Copilot requires a paid Microsoft 365 plan, and it can't send reminder emails on its own.

If you send invoices to clients, you know the awkward feeling of chasing payments. A clean tracker turns that into a 30-second glance. With Copilot in Excel, you describe what you want in everyday words and watch a working tracker appear — no manual formula-writing, no fiddly formatting. This guide is for small-business owners, freelancers, and anyone who wants a simple "who owes me, and how late" view without buying accounting software.

## Before you start
- A paid Microsoft 365 subscription that includes Copilot — either Copilot Pro for personal use, or Copilot for Microsoft 365 for business. Check Microsoft's official pricing page for the current plans and what's included.
- Excel on Windows, Mac, or the web. Some Copilot features vary slightly between desktop and web.
- About 15–20 minutes for the first build; faster once you have a template.
- A handful of real invoices to type in (even three to five rows is enough to test the formulas).

## Step 1 — Open a new workbook and open the Copilot panel
Open Excel and start a **blank workbook**. Look for the **Copilot** button near the top-right of the ribbon, usually marked with a small sparkle or four-pointed-star icon ✨. Click it once. A **chat panel slides open on the right side** of the screen with a short welcome message and a few suggested prompts. If you don't see a Copilot button, your plan almost certainly doesn't include it — that's the most common reason this step fails. As a fallback, try the menu **Home → Copilot**, or look in the ribbon for any tab labelled "Copilot".
💬 Example: type "What can you do?" in the panel just to confirm it's working.
You'll know it worked when a chat panel appears on the right and Copilot replies to your first message.

## Step 2 — Ask Copilot to design the table
Click into cell **A1** of the new workbook so Copilot knows where to start. In the Copilot panel, type a request describing the columns you want. Copilot usually proposes a sample table and asks if you want to insert it — confirm and the columns appear across row 1, with example data in row 2. If your version of Copilot asks you to add at least one row of data first, just type a single fake invoice in row 2 and try again.
💬 Example: "Create a table with columns: Client, Invoice Number, Invoice Date, Due Date, Amount, Status, Days Overdue."
You'll know it worked when seven column headers appear in row 1, formatted as a table with filter dropdowns on each header.

## Step 3 — Fill in your real invoices
Click into the cells under each header and type your actual invoice details. The table **grows automatically** as you type — the filter arrows move down with you. For dates, type them in a form Excel recognizes, like **15 March 2026** or **3/15/2026**, and Excel will store them as real dates. For amounts, type just the number and Excel handles the rest. If the filter dropdowns didn't appear after Step 2, click anywhere in your data and press **Ctrl + T** to convert the range into a proper table.
💬 Example: "Acme Studio | INV-1042 | 1 March 2026 | 31 March 2026 | 1200"
You'll know it worked when you can click the filter arrow on the Client column and see the names you entered.

## Step 4 — Ask Copilot to write the "Days Overdue" formula
With your cursor in the **Days Overdue** column (the cell in row 2 of that column), type a prompt asking Copilot to fill the column with a formula. Copilot usually shows the formula first in the panel — read it. If it makes sense, click **Insert** and the formula appears in the cell, then **auto-fills down** the column. If the formula looks off, ask Copilot to rewrite it; never trust a formula you can't explain in plain English.
💬 Example: "In the Days Overdue column, write a formula that subtracts the Due Date from TODAY(). Show 0 if the date isn't past yet."
You'll know it worked when numbers like **5**, **12**, or **0** appear in the Days Overdue column, with overdue rows showing positive numbers.

## Step 5 — Ask Copilot to color-code the overdue rows
This is the "gentle nudge" part. Ask Copilot to apply **conditional formatting** (rules that automatically colour cells based on their value) based on the Days Overdue column. Copilot typically shows a preview of which cells will be highlighted before applying. Confirm and the formatting sticks. If the prompt doesn't work, do it manually: select the Days Overdue column, go to **Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cell Rules → Greater Than**, and enter **7**.
💬 Example: "Highlight rows red where Days Overdue is more than 7, and yellow where it's between 1 and 7."
You'll know it worked when overdue rows visibly stand out — red for the late ones, yellow for the almost-late ones.

## Step 6 — Save, sort, and (manually) send reminders
Press **Ctrl + S** (Windows) or **⌘ + S** (Mac) and pick a OneDrive or local location. Your tracker is ready to use. Here's the honest limit: **Copilot in Excel cannot send emails automatically**. For the actual nudge, you'll still open Outlook or Gmail, filter your tracker by the red rows, and send a polite follow-up yourself. If you want automatic reminders, you'd need a separate tool — Power Automate, a dedicated invoicing app, or a workflow service — and that's beyond what Excel's Copilot does today.
💬 Example: filter the table by the Status column showing "Overdue" to see your chase list in one click.
You'll know it worked when you can re-open the file tomorrow, sort by Days Overdue, and instantly see who to chase first.

## Common mistakes
- **Trusting a formula you didn't read.** Copilot writes decent formulas, but they're sometimes wrong — wrong column reference, wrong date logic, missing parentheses. Always click the cell and read the formula in the formula bar before trusting the result. If it looks suspicious, ask Copilot to explain it in plain English, or rewrite the prompt.
- **Skipping the plan check.** If Copilot never appears, it's almost always because the account doesn't have Copilot enabled. Confirm your Microsoft 365 plan includes Copilot before troubleshooting anything else — that one check saves an hour.
- **Typing dates as text.** If you type "31 March" without a year, Excel may store it as text and your formulas will break silently. Always include the year, and confirm the column header shows the word "Date" formatting.

## What this means for you
- **If you run a small business or freelance:** You now have a low-effort way to see your cash-flow picture at a glance, and a polite way to know exactly who to chase on Monday morning.
- **If you manage a team or bookkeep for someone else:** This tracker becomes a shared template — anyone with the right Microsoft 365 plan can use it, and the formulas don't need to be rebuilt each time.
- **If you're just getting started:** The simplest first move is to copy the example prompt in Step 2 exactly, then swap in your real column names if you need to.

## Try it now
Open a blank Excel workbook, click the Copilot button, and paste this exact prompt: **"Create a table with columns: Client, Invoice Number, Invoice Date, Due Date, Amount, Status, Days Overdue."** See what Copilot proposes before you change anything — that's the fastest way to feel how it works.
